title: Mohair Lace Shawl
subtitle: Shell lace on a chain-space net in lace weight mohair-silk blend on a 4mm hook
excerpt: A triangular shawl in lace weight mohair-silk blend worked on a 4mm hook for an intentionally open, halo-textured fabric. The pattern is shell lace over a chain-space net: each row of treble shells sits over the chain spaces of the row below.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Shell lace over chain-net construction is a well-established technique with no single originating source.
heroPrompt: A delicate triangular lace shawl in dusty rose mohair-silk yarn. The fabric has a soft halo and open shell pattern. Draped over a pale wooden hanger against a white plaster wall. Soft daylight.

glossaryTerms.definition: A foundation fabric made of chains and double crochets spaced to create a grid of large holes. On the next row, pattern stitches such as shells are worked into the holes rather than into individual stitches.
A group of treble crochets worked into the same stitch or chain space to form a fan shape. In this pattern each shell is 5 trebles worked into a single chain space.

content.text: This shawl is a top-down triangle. It measures approximately 140cm across the top edge and 70cm from the top to the lower point. The pattern uses two row types, worked in turns. A chain-net row creates open chain spaces. A shell row follows, placing 5-treble fans into those spaces. The 4mm hook is bigger than you would normally use for lace weight yarn. This is intentional: it opens the mesh, softens the drape, and lets the mohair halo show. Mohair is less stretchy than wool. Count your stitches at the end of each row. Fix mistakes before moving on, as unpicking mohair is harder than unpicking wool.

Mohair-silk blends shed fibres into each other as you work. Cut yarn cleanly with sharp scissors and soak ends in a tiny amount of hair conditioner before weaving in if the yarn is particularly slippery.

Yarn: approximately 200g of lace weight mohair-silk blend. These yarns are very light so 200g goes further than it sounds. Hook: 4mm (used oversize deliberately). You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, tape measure, a foam blocking mat, and rust-proof pins.
Gauge

One shell repeat (5 tr into a chain space) measures approximately 5cm wide on a 4mm hook with lace weight mohair-silk. The open gauge is intentional. Do not adjust to a smaller hook to tighten the fabric: the structure of the pattern depends on the chain spaces remaining open.
Stitches used
ch: chain
dc: double crochet (UK)
tr: treble crochet (UK)
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp
Chain net: dc + ch-3 sp alternating to form the open grid
sl st: slip stitch
Pattern

The shawl starts at the top centre. The pattern alternates between a net row (which creates the open chain spaces) and a shell row (which fills them). The triangle grows by one shell at each edge on every shell row.
Foundation
Ch 8, sl st to form a ring.
Row 1 (RS): first shell row
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in ring (half-shell at edge), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (shell), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (edge), turn. (3 shells, 4 ch-3 sps)
Row 2 (WS): net row

Ch 5 (counts as dc + ch 3), dc in centre tr of first shell, [ch 3, dc in ch-3 sp, ch 3, dc in centre tr of next shell] across, ch 3, dc in top of turning ch, turn. (creates ch-3 sps over each shell and between)
Row 3 (RS): shell increase row

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in first ch-3 sp (new edge shell), [ch 3, dc in next ch-3 sp, ch 3, shell in next ch-3 sp] across, 4 tr in last ch-3 sp (new edge shell), tr in last dc, turn. (adds 1 shell at each edge)
Continuing

Alternate Row 2 (net row) with Row 3 (shell increase row). Each shell row adds 2 shells to the total. Continue until the top edge measures approximately 140cm. At the stated gauge this is approximately 14 full shell rows (28 rows total), with approximately 29 shells across the final shell row. End with a net row.
Final edging
Work one final row of dc along the top edge only, placing 1 dc per stitch and 1 dc per chain space for a neat finished edge. Fasten off.
Finishing

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Because mohair halo fibres interlock, ends can be trimmed close after weaving. Block thoroughly: soak in cool water for 15 minutes, press out excess moisture in a towel (do not wring), and pin to the stated dimensions on a foam mat. Pin each shell open at its full width. The halo will bloom and the triangular shape will set properly only once fully dry.
Care

Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent suitable for mohair. Do not agitate or the fibres will felt. Press out moisture in a towel, reshape, and dry flat. Re-block after each wash to restore the triangular shape.
What to try next

For a similar shell-over-chain construction in a more forgiving yarn, the classic prayer shawl uses DK weight with the same principle. For a lace shawl with more complex stitch work in the same weight yarn, the baby christening shawl uses a 2.5mm hook for a much finer, closer fabric. If you want to continue with mohair, a simple dc-mesh scarf on the same 4mm hook will give you more practice managing the yarn without a stitch pattern to track.
